title: What level of AI graphical assistance is acceptable to you?

posts.author: Garryg
posts.body:
I've seen a lot of people dismissing anything remotely touched by AI as just inherently wrong. But there is a huge range of different AI tools available now. With many graphics designing applications including AI based tools that are functionally similar to more traditional algorithm based tools the results of some AI can be indistinguishable form other drawing methods.
So where do you draw the line?
If someone draws a character or tile set by hand then touches it up with AI tools is that considered to be AI graphics?
What about the other way around. Someone uses AI to get ideas for graphics then ether heavily modifyes those graphics or makes their own based on the AI generated graphics. Is that still AI graphics to you?
Under the law nether of those images would be considered AI and copyright would default to the maker.

To me it seems like you are mistaking a marketing teams use of a standard algorithm where they branded it as "AI"
Just like a toaster that says it'll toast the perfect bread using "AI" except it's using the same dumb set of sensors we've been using for decades.
To be clear, what I am talking about and what I think most people assume you are talking about is Generative AI. Going forward when I refer to AI, I'm talking about that.
Not every software now includes it, and those that do may just spin an old algorithm as AI. For example, I do music. My software limiter has had for the past decade a "optimize loudness" function that listens to the song and automatically sets the limiter level. In a recent update they changed it to "AI enhanced loudness" but it functions exactly the same way and gives the same results. In both cases, it's always done a poor job, so I just limit the track myself. Limiters are one of the easier tools to use, but that's beside the point.
So, as you said yourself:
Garryg said:
I think not all AI is what you think it is.
Click to expand...
Sometimes it comes down to old school algorithms and not a predictive neural network.
edit:
I also wanted to add on - while this might be different per creative outlet per person - as someone who has done music basically my whole life, I enjoy the whole process. It might be the 100th time I crafting another farty sounding synth sound, but that's fun! It might be the 200th time I am putting a 4-on-the-floor drum pattern, but there still fun to be had there. I've always struggled to come up with good melodies, but even with the hardest part of song making, I enjoy noodling on my keyboard until I finally find something that fits.
Some of the tools I have seen that are legitimate GenAI packages that come with software are often about reducing the grunt work; quickly getting you to a starting point. And I guess if that's all that is used, I'm fine with it if others want to use it.
But to me, a lot of my own music evolves as I go through the grunt work; the way the sounds are programmed influences the way the drums are placed, influencing the way the melody will sound. Every part builds off of the last thing.
So I can say as a creative who has had softwares market their "AI Shortcut tools" to me, it's not something I am interested in.
And I feel like most creatives who have been doing their artwork all their life likely feel the same way. The difference between fancy new tools of the past - like my pixel artist using something like Pixel Composer - compared to AI is that the old software tools have empowered my artist to do things that would have been far too tedious in the past to make practical to do (particle effects, noise generation, and noise generation algorithms) while AI often touts taking away parts of that process. It doesn't empower, it just...well...enshittifies the process.
Tech bros who make this stuff don't understand creatives. They think creatives just
want
their art to magically be finished, when in truth most of us
want
to struggle through the process of making something. As the old saying goes:
It's about the journey, not the destination.

So, I will chime in here at the risk of making people angry with my opinion. But as my generation likes to say...It is what it is.
With any technical advancement, there are going to be impacts on people's jobs. I would love to hear a single example of a significant technical advancement that didn't end up displacing some workers in jobs that become irrelevant. I certainly can't think of any.
Now, for those impacted, that always sucks. But to the general public who isn't impacted, they are more focused on the improvements that come with advancement.
AI is no different in that general context. AI is going to eliminate certain jobs. Probably more than most other technical advancements in human history. And humans will have to adapt.
Why do I say all this?
Because with AI, I fall into the general public category that is more focused on the improvements and benefits rather than the impact on jobs.
And yes, I have the privilege to do that because of my age, where I live, my financial situation etc.
So, personally, I don't have any problems with using AI as a tool. I don't like that AI is using other people's works without their permission. I think that was a bad call on those creating AI. I think there is plenty of public domain content that could be used without the current debate being triggered.
Now, out of respect for the people who have helped me with developing my current Sudoku game and whose assets I'm using, I won't use any AI assets in my game. Even if personally I think some of the graphics would look better using AI.
In fact, when I conceived of using categories of backgrounds for my puzzles, I based that on images that I saw and really liked BEFORE I understood that there was this debate and conflict over using AI images and that the images I liked were created with AI.
So, I spent hours and hours searching for backgrounds to fill my categories that weren't generated with AI. It wasn't easy.
So, again. I won't be using any AI assets in my Sudoku game. Out of respect for those from this forum who I will credit as contributing with either assets or programming assistance. Because I don't know how they would feel being credited (associated even tangentially) with a project/game that uses AI.
And since my Sudoku game will end up being free, I don't want to pay money to commission assets for use in a free game. Maybe in a future game.
In fact, I will state that given the choice between working with a human artist and using AI, I would much rather work with the human artist. But as a hobby developer who might not make any real money even if I someday try to make a commercial game, I probably wouldn't want to pay to commission assets.
I would gladly work in partnership with artists who would take a share of potential money from sales. And I would be happy to consider asking other artists if they would be willing to engage in such an arrangement AFTER I had a full game made with placeholders. Then they could gauge for themselves whether or not the game has sufficient potential for them to be part of the project in a profit sharing arrangement. I think that is entirely different than people who try such an arrangement when they haven't even shown that they can successfully make a game.
So, in summary. I don't necessarily have a problem with using AI as a tool, as needed. And I foresee the entire landscape being fundamentally changed within the next 10 years.
But I also respect those who don't like using AI, who don't want to purchase products made with AI, and I do sympathize with the literally hundreds of thousands of people who will be directly impacted by the increase in AI that will eliminate entire categories of jobs in the future.
I'm just very glad that I'm not just starting out in my career and that in less than a year, I will be fully retired instead of just semi-retired.
Again, I hope that this doesn't make people angry and that they can appreciate my right to have my perspective. If not, and this impacts how people want to engage with me in the future, I will just say again...It is what it is.
I'm too old to be concerned about sharing my opinion for fear that people won't be willing to help me in the future.
I wish everyone good luck on their projects and remember to enjoy what you do!

Contextualizing:
AI-Assisted Graphics is more powerful in the context of a professional project (such as the development of an indie game), not because AI is smarter, but because it combines the speed of AI with the precision and control of the human artist.
AI-Assisted Graphics is the working methodology (the practical use).
What it is: The intentional and targeted use of Generative AI tools and other AIs in a design workflow controlled by a human.
Example: The artist takes the AI-generated "lush forest" image, takes it to Photoshop, resizes it to 960 x 720 pixels, slices it to create the three Parallax layers (Base, Below, Above), and uses Content-Aware Fill (also AI) to remove an unwanted tree.
Traditionally, a "super indie game" made by a single person (so-called solo-devs) required years of hard work, as in classic examples: Stardew Valley (primarily made by Eric Barone), Undertale (Toby Fox), or A Lenda do Herói (Dumativa, which took years to achieve success).
The young person who started following generative AI in 2022 (when it exploded in popularity) and who has 4 years of game development experience (until the end of 2025) is in a unique and extremely advantageous position.
I personally don't know this type of AI, but I think it would be very useful; I think it would cut the development of any game in half.

As an artist I would draw the line at: no generative AI at all. Let me help you understand this point of view a little better by clearing up some common misconceptions that were previously stated in this thread.
"AI learns just like humans, inspired by other people's work."
Not true at all! For art the AI learns patterns of pixels, not concepts and ideas. A human artist would benefit a lot from studying anatomy, proportions, and perspective. On the other hand, you can't feed an AI anatomy books and expect it to get better at drawing hands. Essentially a human artist is inspired by other works, but uses their knowledge of perspective and anatomy to make a completely unique image. AI needs millions of images to take patterns from before it can draw it. For example there were instances where people were struggling to generate a burger without cheese because most images the AI consumed had cheese. It couldn't do something so simple as remove the cheese until more images were added to the training data. Also very interesting that AI models degrade in quality when consuming other AI generated images.
"So you hate it and call it slop because it's stealing your job?"
Nope, that's not the reason people call it slop. The reason is because it is slop. It may be good at producing a single image, but anything more complicated and it becomes very apparent. Inconsistent art styles, wordy and over-explained dialogue, glitches everywhere. Like an old rm2k project which uses assets from 13 different games. A game is very complicated and a massive creative undertaking and Gen AI is just not good enough. Even just the writing part, it's good with grammar and prose, but the dialogue and substance of the story just turns out extremely boring, as if written by a 10 year old (I've tried many gen AI for story writing myself). Lol I looked it up before posting to make sure I was correct. Even ChatGPT ratted itself out. Here's some quotes from it.
1.
"AI image generation works by training models on vast datasets of images and their corresponding text descriptions. When a user provides a text prompt, the AI uses its
learned patterns
to translate that text into a visual representation."
2.
"To create a new image, the model starts with random noise. It then uses its
learned patterns
to progressively remove the noise, step-by-step, until the noise is transformed into an image that matches the text prompt."
Basically the AI is taking small pieces of art from millions of non-consenting artists and mashing them into one new artwork.
Click to expand...
You misunderstood what that means. Those 'learned patterns' are not pixel patterns. It learns weighted node patterns to determine what something is and to reconstruct it mathematically. No actual parts of real images or pixels are ever involved, stored or reused at all.
You would need to learn deeper than that to understand the nuance of that that sentience actually means.
The 'patterns' referred to in both sentences are not what you interpreted then as they are weighted nodes within the AI matrix (database if you like). A lot of people have the same bias. It's common.
Chat GTP can explain this information to you, but it starts of very surface level which is very open to the wrong conclusions. Chat bots openly try to tell the user what they want to know first sometimes to the detriment of actual information. Do not use general Chat bot AI for any real research, they aren't good at it! I would not advocate for learning from a 'normal' chatbot as you often need to already know the very specific questions to ask in order to get specific and actually useful answers!

why does it also add the signatures of the images they took the data from?

First off AI art doesn't store any images. It does not take 'image' data directly. It looks at thousands of like images and determines a mathematical model for what something should look like. In the case of paintings these generally have signatures. So when asked to reproduce a picture, especially a painting 'in the style of' it makes (determines) a logical model (no 'stolen' pixels involved) of what that image should look like, and part of that image is the 'squiggly line bit at the bottom.' AI does not 'think' it is not sentient in any way. It purely understands that this request generally has that marking at the bottom and reproduces it as a part of the image.
Again understanding this shows that no 'steeling' or forgery is implicit from the actual AI.

Only a work produced by a human can be copyrighted. That law existed before the advent of AI.
Any painting by a machine or animal cannot be copyrighted ether.
To prove copyright of an AI derived work a human must provide sufficient evidence of 'creative control and change' in a court of law.
if it's not stealing, why is tracing stealing, even though you actuallyy need human input on it?
Click to expand...
Because tracing is a direct 'copy' of an existing work. AI 'art' does not directly copy any individual works. It merely makes a model of what those things should look like in general. And tries to construct an image based on a prompt. Even in youre example above that is not a direct copy by how the AI works. Instances are generally a forced output by a human trying to force a point.
The output may be exactly what the user (not Artist or Author, USER) wants but may be totally different!
I am actually all in favour of much more regulation in how AI is used, so the above can't be forced to happen, especially where 'whole image' generative AI is concerned.
I would just like for people to have a clear idea of what it is and isn't. What it does and doesn't do. If you still hate it based on what I said, fine you are obviously allowed to. Just hate it for the proper real reasons!
To be clear the only current 'legal' debate on AI use is a small very specific issue that will have massive implications when a ruling is finally made ether way. It concerns the fact that currently all 'scraped' or studied data must be temporarily copied on to a server by the AI in order for it to be analysed (ingested). Immediately after that analysing the original source is dropped.
The AI itself retains no direct copy of the input only the mathematical (probability weightings) model data it added based on the original source. The data the AI retains in NOT itself in any legal ambiguity (it is perfectly legal to hold this as it is counted as derived "knowledge" not copyed data).
Only the process of initially copying the source material, which is currently clamed under the various 'fair use' and Text and Data Mining (TDM) type laws around the world. This very specific aspect is not what people generally refer to when they say AI copying is an issue!

As AI 'quality of life' functions are now becoming ubiqutouse in mainstream Art packages in general like Photoshop (e.g. effects, lighting/colouring, dithering etc) how do you intent to navigate this new reality? I am specificaly NOT talking about 'whole picture' AI Generative apps here.
The industry is not just changing, a lot of it has already changed, with an estimated 60% of marketing and 45% of graphic designers now actively using AI tools in their daily work.
This is not a jibe, I am genuinely interest in your approach to this.

posts.author: Prescott
posts.body:
For graphical assets specifically, I think just using generated stuff wholesale is the main point people have a problem with. Using AI to do things that typically other tools would have done in the past is totally fine and people who see an issue with that should go back to drawing on a canvas with brushes paints. I'm talking about things like edge detection, upscaling, and other general workflow things. Just like older tools you'll still have to make sure it actually looks good at the end though, and that's where a lot of people just really have a major failing because they lack the skill to make sure it looks good.
I also don't mind generated art being used for placeholders, idea crafting, pose references, things like that. Traditionally, that sort of thing would just be using straight up copyrighted material and/or actual humans' likenesses anyway and they aren't meant for the final product. In many cases they aren't even meant for much beyond the planning stages. It is far easier and more productive to give a description of a character to an AI, fine tune some things with it, and then present it to an artist for them to work off of than to go scouring seven different image websites and gathering a bunch of pieces to cobble together to show an artist, and in that case you're doing essentially what an AI would do but in a much less efficient and accurate manner.
I have done something recently where I had a specific style in mind but could not for the life of me find what I was looking for, only things that got kind of close to it, so I grabbed those, plugged them in to an AI, and told it to change the image based on the kind of style I wanted until it actually got there. Showed that to the artist and what I was trying to describe to them earlier was made WAY more clear.
Using it as a tool is completely fine and honestly should be relatively encouraged. It'll make you faster, more efficient, and as long as you aren't relying on it entirely and still know your way around what it is you are using it for, it'll be a great tool to have. In a perfect world, places like AAA game studios adopting the use of AI for things like brute force testing would heavily decrease costs and development time so we would get games faster and cheaper, but I expect it to be poorly implemented and most of the savings are just going to go straight to the top.
Don't blame the tool, blame the user. Above all else, remember that you are still making something for human consumption, as well. A robot is good for doing robotic things extremely well, but only a human is going to be able to make things for a human at the end of the day, with or without the robot's help.

I would agree to a point. After all, the final design of all characters in my game was based on earlier ai renditions.
As Dextera Mortis originally started as I book I tried to write 15 years ago, I had descriptions and a general idea of what they should look like. Ai helped me but those ideas to an image. And those images were then given to an artist to help them understand to a point what I wanted these characters to look like.
Ai has definitely been a help with my creativity. While I am even kinda bad as a prompter and had to go through countless iterations to find an image that reflected my idea of the characters, it was ultimately my decision on which artworks to pick and which to discard. That is still a creative process.
I even think most criticisms against ai is ridiculous. For example the art theft argument. Thing is, regardless of the training data used, I cannot for the life of my identity which images were used in a piece of generative ai art, and I bet neither can anyone else. The fact that the result is distinct from the material in the training data makes it a transfirmative work in my opinion and therefore fair use. We don't think it is a problem when a human gets inspired by the work of other artists, so why is this a problem for machines?
Not to mention how ai technology has made making passable art for even the most unskilled human who might want to express ideas they otherwise never could. Huge boon in my book.
Granted there are other aspects of its use I don't agree with. Like when big companies use mediocre ai artwork instead of hiring actual artists. This can be excused when someone with little funds or resources use ai because they can't draw, nor afford to hire artists. But when a company that has millions of dollars in resources does it, they are just being cheap.
I think companies are jumping the gun a bit, sure, ai is impressive in many ways even now. But it is yet not a match for even a mediocre artist. Humans can outdo ai when it comes to art at least quite easily. Ai cannot even truly create a new style, it can only copy what has come before. So humans will always be needed to iterate and create new styles and ideas. After all, without all that training data, art done by actual humans, ai would not be able to do anything at all. Ai can only really replace lower skilled people, it is only passable, not great, true masters simply produce better work than machines.
This technology is ultimately built on the combined excellence of all of humanity throughout history and it would be nothing without it. Even in a world where using ai is the norm, humans are still needed to provide a blueprint.
Also, what happened to just make art because enjoy making it? Who cares if a machine does it faster. The point is expressing yourself and your ideas. Art is not about owning ip's or making money, but the creative process itself. Ai might be able to write a book, but it will never be my book.
Reminds me of when one of my artists (who is also an rpg maker dev) offered to make my game for me for a fee. I told them no as that would defeat the entire purpose of making your own game.

I agree with pretty much everything you said except this part.
From what I have experienced, this depends entirely on what AI image generator is being used. There are some very simple and crappy AI image generators out there. But there are also some fantastic AI image generators that can make some stunning AI images. It really depends on the generator and the person using it as the tool it is meant to be.
Just like people can use RPG Maker to make crappy games or truly fantastic games.
When AI generated images were first being promulgated, it was quite easy for me to tell what was made with AI. That is no longer true.
Every day I see AI generated images that I would have no way of telling that it was made with AI unless I was told. You could take two images and put them side by side (one AI generated and one drawn by a human) and I wouldn't be able to tell them apart.
I honestly think that is an enormous problem. We need a way to be able to definitively tell if an image was made with AI. Even if it is something embedded in the image itself.
Going back to the OP, I would say that if you are doing this as a hobby and not for making a living off of commercial games, then use whatever resources and tools are at your disposal and that make you happy with your project.
If you are going the commercial route, I personally don't have any problem with you using an resource or tool at your disposal, including AI. Just like I don't have a problem with someone using plugins that they couldn't possibly create on their own and that they don't even understand how they work.
Or someone using RPG Maker because they can't use another game developing engine that doesn't have all the user friendly, preprogrammed Events that make it super simple without knowing any amount of coding.
I am at a point of "You do you, Buttercup" and be happy with your decisions.
Although, I do have an issue with big corporations using substandard assets for the sake of efficiency or budget. No matter what you use, it needs to be good if you are charging a bunch of money for it.
Anyway, just my opinion.

You know what AI is helping me with right now? I'm having it scan my project for everything. Started out with spelling errors and wrong plugin commands and notetags and such. Was really great for knowing I messed up some YEP notetags and figuring out why my convoluted skills chains don't work even when they involve so many plugins.
